title: Your Coding Agent Should Do AI System Engineering — Ben Burtenshaw, Hugging Face
talk_summary: Ben Burtenshaw shows coding agents doing AI systems engineering across three escalating autonomy levels: interactive CUDA kernel writing with file-based skills, zero-shot fine-tuning, and a multi-agent 'AutoLab' research loop (researcher/planner/workers/reporter) that iterates on training scripts against a verifiable metric. The transferable core is not the ML domain but the orchestration pattern: role-split agents, a shared job queue, a reviewer that rejects duplicates/stale ideas, a single shared storage bucket, and a fully open data layer for dashboards.

takeaways.technique: Role-split research loop with planner queue and reviewer gate
takeaways.what_they_do: A researcher agent scouts papers and turns ideas into hypotheses; a planner maintains a job queue; worker agents pick up hypotheses and implement them as patches; a reporter monitors jobs and maintains a dashboard. A reviewer agent rejects duplicate or stale ideas before they enter the queue.
takeaways.evidence_quote: use reviewer to reject duplicates or stale ideas

takeaways.technique: Explicit job-queue data structure in the repo as shared state
takeaways.what_they_do: The main branch holds the training scripts plus a data structure that records scores and the job list; each experiment is a branch with a patch. Agents read and write this queue instead of passing context peer-to-peer.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we have a data structure in the main branch that we use to just keep the scores

takeaways.technique: Open data layer instead of dashboard-only metrics
takeaways.what_they_do: They use Trackio, which stores metrics as plain parquet, so agents can query the raw data directly and build any visualization rather than being limited to a UI's API.

takeaways.technique: Project-maintained file-based skills, benchmarked with an eval harness
takeaways.what_they_do: Skills are just versioned files with examples and benchmark scripts, maintained inside the project they belong to (not a YOLO shared repo). They use 'upskill' to generate an eval per skill and compare models on accuracy and token use.
takeaways.numbers: 94% speedup cited for a generated Qwen3-8B H100 kernel (compatibility, not SOTA)

takeaways.technique: Per-skill model comparison on accuracy and tokens
takeaways.what_they_do: They benchmark the same skill across GPT-OSS, Kimi, Haiku etc., reporting accuracy and token consumption side by side, then pick the cheaper model that holds accuracy.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Kimmy is more accurate and using less tokens. Haiku is a bit more accurate using less tokens

takeaways.technique: Single shared bucket for all run artifacts
takeaways.what_they_do: They point all agents at one HF bucket so training scripts and artifacts aren't uploaded/downloaded per run.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I want all of the storage to be in the same bucket so that I don't have to upload or download the training scripts every time
